passage:
On the first Monday of each month, Tushar's team at the Pune office held what they called 'bad news tea'. Anyone could bring a problem, a missed deadline or a shortcut someone was tempted by, and whoever flagged the most useful one got first pick of the samosas and a mention in the company newsletter.
Today Ganga raised her hand. 'The new partner wants us to skip two identity checks to sign up clients faster.'
Tushar didn't flinch. 'Thank you. That's a line we've already agreed we won't cross. I'll take it to the review committee.'
Later he opened the note pinned on his laptop screen: three lines he had written when he became team lead. The second read: If I catch myself explaining away a bad feeling, stop and ask someone.
He added today's date beside it.

qa.q: What did the new partner want the team to skip?
qa.a: The partner wanted them to skip two identity checks to sign up clients faster.

qa.q: Why doesn't Tushar flinch at Ganga's news?
qa.a: He decided his lines in advance and trusts the process, so bad news feels like something to handle rather than hide.

qa.q: What in this team's habits guards against drift?
qa.a: Regular 'bad news tea' rewards people for raising problems, a review committee takes them up, and Tushar keeps pre-written lines to check himself against.

qa.q: How might Ganga feel raising the problem in this team?
qa.a: Ganga likely feels safe and even valued, knowing a warning will be thanked and acted on rather than punished.

grounding: It shows a team rewarding honest bad news through a regular forum and a leader who set his lines in advance and watches for explaining away discomfort.

'So what exactly changes?' Keerthana asked, stirring coffee in the office canteen.
'Three things,' Ayesha said. 'An anonymous line that goes to the board, not to managers. Bonuses tied to audit results as well as sales. And every quarter, a prize for whoever raises the most useful bad news.'
'A prize for bad news? The old bosses would have fainted.'
'The old bosses are why we had the recall.'
Keerthana was quiet for a moment. 'I knew about the labels, you know. Back then. I told myself it wasn't my department.'
'Most of us told ourselves something.'
'So how do I stop doing that?'
Ayesha pulled a card from a wallet. 'I wrote my lines down the week I joined. Things I won't sign, whatever the target. When I start explaining something away, I read this.'
Keerthana took a photo of it.

qa.q: Where does the new anonymous line go?
qa.a: It goes to the board, not to managers.

qa.q: What does Keerthana's admission about the labels reveal?
qa.a: It reveals lingering guilt about staying silent before, and a wish not to explain away discomfort again.

qa.q: What could Keerthana do the next time a shortcut is suggested?
qa.a: Keerthana could write down personal lines in advance, like Ayesha's card, check them before signing anything, and use the anonymous line to the board if something still feels wrong.

qa.q: Why might Ayesha answer 'Most of us told ourselves something' instead of judging Keerthana?
qa.a: Ayesha seems to know how the old culture pushed many people to look away, so sharing the blame makes it easier for Keerthana to change instead of feeling ashamed.

grounding: It shows an organisation adding a safe reporting line, reviewing incentives and rewarding bad news, and a person keeping written lines to catch rationalising.

passage:
After what happened at my last company, I made myself a list. I keep it in my wallet, behind my ID: Things I will not do. I will not sign what I haven't checked. I will not change a number to fit a target. I will not tell a customer something I know is misleading.
I wrote it while I was calm, because I'd learned that under pressure my mind gets very good at excuses.
At the startup where I now run compliance, we built the other side too. Anyone can report a concern to an external ethics line, anonymously. Every month we give a small award to whoever flagged the most useful bad news. Last month it was Jomon, who spotted that a sales incentive was nudging people to skip consent forms. We changed the incentive that week.
Sometimes I still catch myself thinking, it's just this once. That phrase is my alarm now. I'm Rekha, and I've learned to listen to it.

qa.q: Where does Rekha keep the list?
qa.a: In my wallet, behind my ID.

qa.q: What does Rekha feel on catching the thought 'just this once'?
qa.a: Rekha feels a flash of alarm, recognising the start of explaining away discomfort.

qa.q: Which safeguards at the startup guard best against drift?
qa.a: An anonymous external ethics line, rewarding useful bad news, and quickly changing incentives that push people to cut corners.

qa.q: What might Jomon feel receiving the award?
qa.a: Jomon likely feels valued and safe, rewarded instead of punished for raising a concern.

grounding: A compliance lead sets personal lines in advance and builds safe reporting, rewards for bad news and incentive reviews.

passage:
Operations head's note, quarterly review
I want to record what Manjula did this quarter as shift manager at the packaging plant.
When she took over, she noticed that near-miss reports had dropped to zero, not because the floor was safer, but because people who reported got extra paperwork and a frown. She changed that. She put a box by the canteen for anonymous reports, and every Monday she reads out one report and what was done about it. She began thanking people in meetings for bad news. When Asif, an operator, reported a guard that kept jamming, Manjula stopped the line within the hour and had it fixed.
She also told her team leads that bonuses would no longer depend only on output, but on safety checks completed honestly.
Near-miss reports went from zero to fourteen. Actual incidents fell. I am recommending her approach for all three plants.

qa.q: How many near-miss reports came in after the change?
qa.a: From zero to fourteen.

qa.q: What might Asif have felt when the line was stopped within the hour?
qa.a: Asif likely felt respected and relieved, seeing that reporting led to action rather than a frown.

qa.q: Why did Manjula's changes work?
qa.a: A safe anonymous channel, thanking people for bad news, fast action, and incentives tied to honest safety checks.

qa.q: How might the team leads feel about the new bonus rules?
qa.a: They may feel unsettled at first but freer to report honestly, since output alone no longer decides their bonus.

grounding: A manager builds safe reporting, rewards honest bad news and reviews incentives, and reported problems rise while incidents fall.

passage:
Sunday evening
Before the new job starts tomorrow, I did what my mentor from last year's internship told me to do: I wrote my lines down in advance.
One: I won't sign a report I haven't read.
Two: If I'm asked to change a number, I'll ask "what's the source?" before anything else.
Three: If I catch myself saying "everyone does it" or "it's only this once", I'll stop and sleep on it.
Four: On day one I'll find out where the ethics line is.
Darshan, my new manager, seemed decent in the interview. I hope I never need this list. But last year I watched good people slide, one small step at a time, and not one of them decided to be dishonest. They just never decided where their line was.
I've stuck the list inside my notebook cover. It feels a bit dramatic. It also feels like armour.
Shalini

qa.q: What is line three on Shalini's list?
qa.a: If I catch myself saying 'everyone does it' or 'it's only this once', I'll stop and sleep on it.

qa.q: How does Shalini feel about the list?
qa.a: Shalini feels a little self-conscious but reassured, as if the list were armour.

qa.q: Why is writing the lines before the job starts wise?
qa.a: Deciding limits in advance, while calm, makes it easier to notice when pressure starts explaining away discomfort.

qa.q: What might Darshan think on seeing the list?
qa.a: Darshan might feel impressed, or a little uneasy, seeing a new hire who has thought carefully about integrity.

grounding: Before starting a new job, a young professional decides personal lines in advance and plans to notice when discomfort is being explained away.

[Friday, 6:15 pm]
Keerthana: Vijay, did you see the email about the new reporting line?
Vijay: Yes. Anonymous, goes straight to the outside ethics firm. Finally
Keerthana: And that "good catch" award for whoever flags a problem early 👏
Vijay: I nearly laughed. Two years ago you'd get moved to the basement for that
Keerthana: I'm still going to write my list though
Vijay: What list?
Keerthana: The one the trainer suggested. Three things I won't do, whatever the target. Written before I'm under pressure
Vijay: Okay what's on yours
Keerthana: 1. Sign for a check I didn't see. 2. Change a date on anything. 3. Tell a customer something I know is false
Vijay: Good one. Mine would add: notice when I start saying "it's just this once"
Keerthana: That's the sneaky one 😅
Vijay: Yeah. I said it three times last quarter
Keerthana: Then that's your line 🙂

qa.q: What are the three things on Keerthana's list?
qa.a: Sign for a check I didn't see, change a date on anything, and tell a customer something I know is false.

qa.q: How does Vijay seem to feel about the new reporting line?
qa.a: Vijay feels relieved and a bit amazed, remembering that two years ago people who flagged problems were punished.

qa.q: Why is writing the list before pressure a wise step?
qa.a: Deciding the lines in advance means Keerthana and Vijay can recognise a bend when it comes, instead of explaining it away in the moment.

qa.q: What might it be like for Vijay to admit saying it's just this once three times?
qa.a: Vijay may feel a little embarrassed but also honest and lighter, because naming it with a friend makes it easier to catch next time.

grounding: Shows an organisation creating a safe reporting line and rewarding early bad news, while individuals set their lines in advance and watch for explaining away discomfort.
